query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A post‐processing heat treatment that induces controlled, fine-scale ordering (γ′-like precipitates) and grain refinement in a titanium‐ and nickel‐rich single‐phase high‐entropy alloy will enhance its elevated‐temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the same alloy in its as-processed (coarse-grained, no significant precipitation) state.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase FCC solid solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents, typically exhibiting a relatively coarse grain structure and lacking any significant nanoscale precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a tailored heat-treatment protocol comprising a solutionizing step at high temperature followed by rapid quenching and a controlled aging treatment. This process is designed to induce the nucleation of fine, uniformly distributed ordered precipitates (γ′-like phase, e.g., Ni3Ti-type) and to reduce the grain size.
generation.conditions: The alloy composition remains focused on high concentrations of Ti and Ni (with accompanying elements such as Co, Fe, Cr, etc.), processed by methods like additive manufacturing or powder metallurgy. Mechanical performance is evaluated under elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 700–1000 °C) via tensile and creep tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a fine-scale, ordered precipitate structure (γ′ phase) within a refined matrix. The resultant microstructure features both a higher density of strengthening interfaces and a reduced grain size.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale γ′ precipitates increase the anti-phase boundary energy and act as barriers that impede dislocation motion (ordering strengthening), while the refined grain structure provides additional strengthening via the Hall–Petch mechanism. Together, these effects reduce dislocation mobility at high temperatures and delay the onset of creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit higher yield strengths and longer creep rupture lives at elevated temperatures. Its refined microstructure and uniform precipitate dispersion should also improve thermal stability and resistance to grain coarsening.
generation.baseline: The as-processed (e.g., as-deposited or as-sintered) titanium- and nickel-dominant high-entropy alloy that exists as a single coarse-grained FCC solid solution without engineered precipitation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to alloys within the titanium- and nickel-rich high-entropy family, tested predominantly under high-temperature regimes (approximately 700–1000 °C). The treatment parameters must be controlled to avoid the formation of unwanted deleterious phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise heat-treatment temperatures, durations, and quench rates required to optimize the precipitate size, volume fraction, and grain structure are not fully established and may require further optimization. Stability of these precipitates under prolonged service at elevated temperatures also remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium- and nickel-rich high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to the proposed heat-treatment protocol (solution treatment, rapid quench, and controlled aging) and leave the other set in the as-processed state. Conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (tensile tests and creep tests) in the 700–1000 °C range. Analyze microstructures using SEM, EDS, and TEM to quantify grain sizes and precipitate distributions.
measurements: Microhardness (as a proxy for overall strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance compared to the untreated alloy, or if microstructural analysis reveals the formation of deleterious phases or insufficient precipitation/grain refinement, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The exceptional mechanical properties of Ni-based high entropy alloys are due to the presence of ordered L12 (γ′) precipitates embedded within a disordered matrix phase. While the strengthening contribution of the γ′ phase is generally accepted, there is no consensus on the precise contribution of the individual strengthening mechanisms to the overall strength. In addition, changes in alloy composition influence several different mechanisms, making the assessment of alloying conditions complex. Multicomponent L12-ordered single-phase alloys were systematically developed with the aid of CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations. The alloying elements Co, Cr, Ti, and Nb were chosen to complexify the Ni3Al structure. The existence of the γ′ single phase was validated by microstructure characterization and phase identification. A high-temperature compression test from 500 °C to 1000 °C revealed a positive temperature dependence of strength before reaching the peak strength in the studied alloys NiCoCrAl, NiCoCrAlTi, and NiCoCrAlNb. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. AbstractThe focus of this study is the evaluation of the influence of Ti concentration on the tensile properties of powder metallurgy high entropy alloys. Three Ni1.5Co1.5CrFeTiX alloys with X = 0.3; 0.5 and 0.7 were produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. Additional annealing heat treatment at 1100 °C was utilized to obtain homogenous single-phase face centered cubic (FCC) microstructures, with minor oxide inclusions. The results show that Ti increases the strength of the alloys by increasing the average atomic size misfit i.e., solid solution strengthening. An excellent combination of mechanical properties can be obtained by the proposed method. For instance, annealed Ni1,5Co1,5CrFeTi0.7 alloy possessed the ultimate tensile strength as high as ~1600 MPa at a tensile ductility of ~9%, despite the oxide contamination. The presented results may serve as a guideline for future alloy design of novel, inclusion-tolerant materials for sustainable metallurgy.Keywords: multi principal element alloy, tensile strength, fracture, ductility, powder
